newsitem.title: USA: Political killings rose in Haiti, U.S. says.
newsitem.headline: Political killings rose in Haiti, U.S. says.

text.p: Political killings by Haitian authorities rose last year from 1995, but remained far fewer than in the years leading up to the U.S. military operation that restored Haiti's first democratically elected president, the United States said on Thursday.

"Political and extrajudicial killings by the authorities increased slightly in 1996 compared with 1995, while remaining far fewer than during the 1991-94 period," when a military junta ruled after ousting President Jean-Bertrand Aristide, the State Department said in its annual survey of human rights.

Despite the increase in political killings, the State Department said Rene Preval, Haiti's second democratically elected president, continued the "significant progress in the transition to democracy that began" with Aristide's restoration to power in October 1994.
"The government generally respected the human rights of its citizens, continuing the overall improvement in the human rights climate since the end of the military regime," the report said.
"However, a significant number of serious abuses occurred, and cases of abuse remained steady in frequency and severity during the course of the year," it said.
It said "persons linked to palace security forces" killed two opposition politicians, and the police killed at least 19 others.
